image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Treemap** (main graphic) showing countries as rectangles sized by historical CO₂ emissions share.  
   - **Stacked bar charts** (bottom) comparing shares of historical CO₂ emissions and population.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.

   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Treemap** (main graphic) showing countries as rectangles sized by historical CO₂ emissions share.  
   - **Stacked bar charts** (bottom) comparing shares of historical CO₂ emissions and population.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Treemap** (main graphic) showing countries as rectangles sized by historical CO₂ emissions share.  
   - **Stacked bar charts** (bottom) comparing shares of historical CO₂ emissions and population.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

1. **Chart type**  
   - **Treemap** (main graphic) showing countries as rectangles sized by historical CO₂ emissions share.  
   - **Stacked bar charts** (bottom) comparing shares of historical CO₂ emissions and population.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

raw_comment: In this graph, the first thing I notice is how the United States is the country that uses the most amount of carbon emissions by such a large difference compared to the other countries. I also was shocked by how only 23 rich countries can use more CO2 emissions than more than 150 countries combined. Finally, I noticed China's 13.9% which was a surprise due to its large size. I wonder why China uses such a far less amount of emissions compared to the other large countries. I also wonder why North Korea's percentage is so low that the chart does not even show the data. This graph impacts me and my community through my own country, the United States, and the number of emissions used. I myself contribute to this percentage through my electricity. A headline that summarizes the data shown in this graph would be, "Countries' Wealth and its Effect on Carbon Emissions."

   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

I also notice that of the 23 rich countries, the U.S. is responsible for nearly half of those emissions. I wonder why 12% of the world's population is responsible for 50% of the CO2 emissions. This is important to my community because I live in the country responsible for the most emissions, which affects climate change. If we don't do anything to reduce our emissions, I won't have a planet to live on.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I noticed that the 23 rich and developed countries are responsible for half in contrast to the other 150 countries, but the population in comparison is much much smaller. The U.S. is mainly responsible for the CO2 emissions for the rich and developed countries, accumulating roughly half of their total carbon emission. You can add up the main contributors on the other 150 countries (China, India, and Russia) and it would still not be equivalent to the U.S. carbon emission. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder how the 23 rich and developed countries accumulated more CO2 emissions despite having a much smaller total population. Does the industrialization and technology of the more developed countries have bridged the gap so much?
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts me and my global community as it demonstrates who in the world is slowly deteriorating our planet. The increase in CO2 emissions can have a negative effect on the atmosphere and ozone layer that protects us from harmful rays and also destroys our world's biodiversity. 
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
This graph shows the historical carbon emissions for the world's 23 richest countries and for all countries. 
"Global Carbon Creators"

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Treemap** (main graphic) showing countries as rectangles sized by historical CO₂ emissions share.  
   - **Stacked bar charts** (bottom) comparing shares of historical CO₂ emissions and population.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

raw_comment:
I'm not surprised that only 23 developed countries take up almost half of the world's CO2 emissions. Historically, the United States was an industrial powerhouse for much of the 20th century, and as a result we created extreme amounts of pollution. The United States also has failed to drastically reduce carbon emissions, so our output is only going to go up. The second thing I noticed was that China is the largest country on the other side of the chart. Though China hasn't been industrially involved that long, in the past decades it has dramatically increased. I know that today China is struggled with air pollution and overall environmental damage from the constant manufacturing. 

I wonder if China will surpass the United States in carbon emissions. How will that affect weather patterns and the environment overall?

This relates to me in my community because the United States is responsible for almost half of all carbon emissions. As a nation, we have a duty to maintain a safe and healthy environment for all of our citizens and their children. The Earth's resources and tolerance for these harmful toxins are slowly diminishing, and it could prove to be an international crisis if we don't act now.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Treemap** (main graphic) showing countries as rectangles sized by historical CO₂ emissions share.  
   - **Stacked bar charts** (bottom) comparing shares of historical CO₂ emissions and population.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

1. Evidently from the graph, developed countries play a significant role in the global carbon emissions. Immediately it is shown that the top 23 developed countries, despite making up 12% of the population, account for 50% of the carbon emissions worldwide. This includes the United States, which leads the emissions in this crisis.
2. The graph makes me wonder if the United States will actually be able to reduce its carbon emissions. President Biden already stated that he will seek to slash carbon emissions in half by 2030; however, if a Republican candidate takes office, will they revert this policy? Additionally, would the Chinese Communist Party be willing to reduce their emissions for the sake of the planet?. Despite being a "developing" nation, the country still boasts the second largest economy and competes with the Untied States. 
3. This relates to my community as New York State plays an important part in the economy of the United States and in turn carbon emissions. Many Long Islanders commute to New York City by car. With the increased traffic in the region, it is clear that our community affects the carbon emissions. 
4. The graph depicts the carbon emissions of the world, splitting countries into two categories, developed and developing countries. The developed countries release 50% of the carbon emissions, despite making a small portion of the population. A catchy headline for the graph would be "Developing Countries Lead the Charge for Carbon Emissions!"

raw_comment:
-What do I notice?

I notice that the United States is the leading contributor to CO2 emissions with a whopping 24.6% in comparison to ALL other countries. Other sources of emissions come from countries that either have a high population (China/India), or are more industrialized/economically developed (Japan, Germany, France).

-What do I wonder?

I wonder what the statistics would be for carbon emissions 20 years from now. Will the United States continue to rely on fossil fuels for energy and allow their carbon emissions to increase, or will we convert to more sustainable sources of energy over time, such as electric vehicles, solar-powered homes, or biomass?

How does this relate to me and my community?

As a citizen of the United States, I feel it’s partly my responsibility to make sure America lowers its carbon emissions. We have already seen the effects of global warming: forest fires, the destruction of antarctic habitats, natural disasters, and the extinction of countless species. If we continue down this path of non-renewable energy, irreparable damage to our planet will occur.

Catchy headline: Don’t Act Aloof, Prevent Imminent Doom And Stop Burning CO2!

WE NOTICE

We noticed that the 23 richest countries make up only 12% of the population. This means somehow the richest 12% of the population produces half of the greenhouse gases.

We also noticed that, even though China is not one of the 23 richest countries, it produces the second most greenhouse gases. This makes sense, because it does a lot of the world’s production and because it is a large country.

Furthermore, we noticed that the graph only takes carbon dioxide into account, but not other greenhouse gases.


WE WONDER

We wonder what criteria a country must fall under to be considered rich and developed. Is richness measured in monetary or natural value? Is it based on the average amount of money per citizen or all of the money that a country has?

We wonder why the United States produces more greenhouse gases than China if China is known for its unclean air and mass production.

We wonder how the graph would change if other greenhouse gases besides carbon dioxide were included.

HOW THIS RELATES TO US

The graph admonishes us to reduce our carbon footprints.

As the U.S. has the greatest carbon dioxide emissions, it shows how much power U.S. citizens like us would have in stopping climate change by changing their actions.

Climate change hits us as teenagers especially hard because we are witnessing first-hand how global warming is affecting us and we will soon be responsible for repairing its harm.

A HEADLINE
The Fault of Rich CO2untries

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Treemap** (main graphic) showing countries as rectangles sized by historical CO₂ emissions share.  
   - **Stacked bar charts** (bottom) comparing shares of historical CO₂ emissions and population.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

|---|---|---|

| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

1. **Chart type**

   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Treemap** (main graphic) showing countries as rectangles sized by historical CO₂ emissions share.  
   - **Stacked bar charts** (bottom) comparing shares of historical CO₂ emissions and population.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |

1. **Chart type**  
   - **Treemap** (main graphic) showing countries as rectangles sized by historical CO₂ emissions share.  
   - **Stacked bar charts** (bottom) comparing shares of historical CO₂ emissions and population.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - The main view uses **two side-by-side treemaps / grouped treemap sections**: **Rich countries** and **All others**.  
   - Within each section, rectangles are **nested/packed** and **sized by value**.  
   - **Color** distinguishes the groups.  
   - The bottom uses **horizontal stacked bars** for summary comparison, including a small separate segment for **International transport**.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country / territory name | Categorical/nominal | Text label inside treemap rectangles |
| Group (Rich countries / All others / International transport) | Categorical/nominal | Section placement, color/hue, bar segment grouping, labels |
| Historical CO₂ emissions share (%) by country/territory | Quantitative | Area of treemap rectangles; numeric text labels |
| Summary measure type (Historical CO₂ emissions vs Population) | Categorical/nominal | Separate stacked bar rows; row labels |
| Share of total within summary bars (%) | Quantitative | Length of stacked bar segments; numeric text labels |
| Country count statement (“23 rich, developed countries”, “More than 150 countries”) | Quantitative | Headline text annotations |
